look_here_first: FLUFFGRASS — LOOK AT GROUND LEVEL: a tiny perennial with pointed white-edged leaves clustered around woolly flowering packets tucked INTO the leafy shoot tips, rather than on raised bare stalks. Follow a connected stem and inspect one mature spikelet: usually 6–12 florets, two long near-equal glumes and a hairy deeply 2-lobed lemma with ONE short awn from its notch. The ligule is hair-fringed, but published ligule lengths conflict; measure an actual opened collar rather than using an absolute length cutoff. Compare Erioneuron pilosum, whose compact woolly heads are held ABOVE the basal leaves on slender, mostly leafless stalks.

best_field_traits: SIZE & HABIT: very low dwarf perennial typically 2–15 cm, growing as a dense rosette-like/tufted or sometimes radiating mat in rocky, dry soil; may develop stolon-like shoots with leaf-and-flower clusters at their ends.

STEM & LEAVES: fine wiry culm internodes, with sharp-pointed, tightly rolled (involute) pale- or white-hardened-edged narrow leaves clustered at shoot tips. True shoot-tip leaves are not necessarily florets.

PANICLE: almost hidden WITHIN those tufted sharp leaves, terminal and sometimes axillary, compact ~1–2 cm; typically 1–5 fertile spikelets clustered together, instead of tall flowering heads on separate naked stalks.

SPIKELET: ~7–13 mm, laterally compressed, generally 6–12 fertile florets inside ONE spikelet. Glumes are 1-veined, almost equal and long, usually about 6–8 mm, sometimes reaching the outer floral tips.

LEMMA: ~3–5 mm, 3-nerved, long-hairy mainly below/along nerves, split deeply into TWO lobes reaching about half the length; ONE straight or curved short awn ~1.5–2.5 mm rises from between those lobes.
LIGULE: very short true FRINGE OF HAIRS at blade/sheath junction, ~0.3–0.5 mm under Kew/GrassBase; not a broad membranous tongue. Different sources vary, so examine actual specimen.

LOOK-ALIKE: Erioneuron pilosum has airy-separated long almost bare flower stalks with terminal hairy clubs, relatively SHORT glumes below first floret and a SHALLOW lemma notch (not a Munroa deeply split lemma).
NAME: Dasyochloa pulchella and Erioneuron pulchellum are historical synonyms of Munroa pulchella. Do not conflate the older Erioneuron pulchellum with current distinct Erioneuron pilosum.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: CONNECTED GROWTH FORM: one 2–15 cm clump with long internodes, prostrate/radiating branch tips and node rooting if present; photograph the same plant from rooted stem to leaf cluster, ruler for size.
LEAFY FASCICLE: whole head with 1–5 tucked-in woolly spikelets shorter than or equaled by immediately surrounding needlelike sharp pale-edged leaves; front and side view.
TRUE COLLAR 20×: 0.3–0.5 mm short ligule HAIR FRINGE, blade/sheath clearly opened with 1-mm ruler; do not mistake longer sheath margin hairs for ligule.
ONE MATURE SPIKELET 10–20×: note 6–12 fertile FLORETS inside ~7–13 mm compressed spikelet; scale and paired glumes visible.
GLUMES AND LEMMA: two near-equal shiny glumes reaching toward end of spikelet and 3–5 mm 3-nerved hairy fertile lemma; dissect instead of relying on pale overall fluff.
LEMMA DEEP NOTCH: two apical lobes split nearly half the lemma and ONE ~1.5–2.5 mm awn emerging from their notch, with measured mm scale.
PAIR WITH ERIONEURON: show an actual mature Erioneuron pilosum glume and shallow notched lemma (not an ordinary seedhead) at the same magnification as Munroa.
crew_field_check: FLUFFGRASS — look at ground level, not above the prairie: a TINY (usually about 2–15 cm tall) perennial with short, wiry, sometimes sprawling/stolon-like stems ending in clustered sharp, silvery-white-edged leaves and a cottony little FLOWERING HEAD NESTLED AMONG THOSE LEAVES. Follow a stem to its leafy tip: the terminal (and sometimes axillary) head holds about 1–5 sessile or very short-stalked spikelets, each with about 6–12 fertile FLORETS. At 10–20× look for two rather equal, relatively LONG pointed GLUMES (often ~6–8 mm), and a separate 3-veined hairy lemma DEEPLY split into two lobes, with ONE stout short AWN between the lobes. The true ligule is a very short hair fringe (~0.3–0.5 mm), not a big membrane. These close-up details are NOT verifiable in the current one-photo original.

HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS / Erioneuron pilosum: low perennial bunch, but SMALL TIGHT PALE CLUB HEADS are carried on LONG, mostly leafless erect stems well ABOVE the short basal leaves. FLUFFGRASS / Munroa pulchella: 1–5 compact woolly spikelets are enclosed WITHIN a whorl/cluster of sharp, sometimes nearly white leaves at the TOP of short stems, often angled down and sometimes rooting at nodes; the leafy flowering fascicle, not just woolly color, is a key distinction. Fluffgrass's two long pointed glumes are about as long as its lower spikelet and its fertile lemma is DEEPLY TWO-LOBED (about half its length) with a single stout awn between lobes. In Erioneuron pilosum the glumes are generally SHORTER than the first floret and the lemma notch is very shallow; both have hairy floral organs and hair-fringe ligules, so neither trait ALONE separates them. Other low tuft grasses and tiny Aristida can look fuzzy in drought; check the enclosed short inflorescence and individual florets under magnification. Older DASYOCHLOA PULCHELLA and ERIONEURON PULCHELLUM refer to this Munroa species, NOT the separate species Erioneuron pilosum.

Start with the WHOLE attached leafy shoot tip and one true mature spikelet. Count FLORETS within the spikelet rather than spikelets tucked together in the head. If only fluffy white heads are visible, remain 'grass sp.' until true leaf and glume / lemma architecture is checked.
In a taxon-comparison lesson, keep clearly named Erioneuron images separate; never silently relabel old Erioneuron pulchellum (a Munroa synonym) as Erioneuron pilosum.

Do not treat either length as securely reconciled.

Until resolved, do not use an absolute ligule length as decisive.

field_id_short_tiles.short: Woolly flower packets tucked into sharp leaves
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look down at the shoot tips: pale pointed leaf clusters surround a compact 1–2 cm head of about 1–5 spikelets. The flowering packets sit WITHIN the leafy fascicle, not at the end of a long naked flowering stalk. The true Munroa panels show verified same-taxon habit and flowering, including a locally archived Texas herbarium voucher; none alone proves all minute organs.
field_id_short_tiles.status: VISIBLE GROSS CUE; SAME-PLANT DETAIL STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · FOLLOW THE ROOTED SHOOT
field_id_short_tiles.details: Trace a rooted perennial crown into short wiry, sometimes radiating stems ending in leaf clusters. Kew describes a dwarf perennial with narrow involute blades about 0.5–1 mm wide, hardened white/cartilaginous margins and sharply pointed tips. The physically archived CC0 Brewster County Texas herbarium sheet provides a preserved rooted specimen reference but does not replace a live same-plant root-to-flower sequence.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENT; CONNECTED LIVE ROOT PHOTO GAP

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS, NOT HEADS
field_id_short_tiles.details: One compact head usually contains 1–5 nearly sessile spikelets. A single mature spikelet is approximately 7–13 mm and typically holds 6–12 fertile florets plus reduced terminal florets. Do not confuse a white tuft, an entire spikelet, and one floret; an attached ripe spikelet with 1-mm ruler is still missing.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE GLUMES FROM LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.details: Kew GrassBase: two near-equal persistent 1-veined glumes about 6–8 mm; fertile lemma about 3–5 mm, hairy below, three-veined, and split into two lobes to roughly 40–50% of its length. ONE 1.5–2.5 mm awn arises from the notch between the lobes. These are published values, not verified image measurements; no microscopic arrows are justified.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.details: Expose the INNER blade–sheath junction and distinguish its actual ligule from neighboring sheath-edge hairs. Kew GrassBase reports a 0.5-mm hair fringe; a federal Western Grass Manual reports roughly 0.3–0.5 mm; a Flora of North America derivative reports 3–5 mm. This unresolved source disagreement means no hard ligule-length threshold is safe. Photograph several voucher-confirmed collars face-on at 10–20× with a 1-mm bar.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · DON'T CONFUSE HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Munroa flowers nested; Erioneuron heads raised
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 7–8 (1-based) depict Erioneuron pilosum for comparison, NOT Munroa. Erioneuron has woolly clubs elevated on mostly bare upright stalks; Munroa encloses its woolly spikelets among pointed shoot-tip leaves. Under 20× Munroa's lemma has a deep notch and long glumes, whereas E. pilosum has a shallow lemma notch and relatively shorter glumes. Do not treat pale color or a hair-fringe ligule as a species-specific shortcut.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD LOOK-ALIKE CUE; MATCHED DISSECTIONS NEEDED
